title: Πλούσιος καὶ βυρσοδέψης
titleEn: The Rich Man and the Tanner
part: The Rich Man and the Tanner (Chambry 309)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 309. Text as printed. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Πλούσιος βυρσοδέψῃ παρῳκίσθη· μὴ δυνάμενος δὲ τὴν δυσωδίαν φέρειν διετέλει ἑκάστοτε αὐτῷ ἐπικείμενος, ἵνα μεταβῇ.
sentences.tr: Plousios byrsodepsēi parōikisthē· mē dynamenos de tēn dysōdian pherein dietelei hekastote autōi epikeimenos, hina metabēi.
sentences.l: A rich man came to be settled next door to a tanner; and not being able to bear the stench, he went on pressing him at every turn, that he might move away.
sentences.i: A rich man came to live next door to a tanner; and being unable to bear the stench, he was for ever at him to move.
sentences.n: παρῳκίσθη is passive in form but says only where the man came to live; Greek uses the passive of παροικίζω for taking up residence beside someone. διατελέω with a supplementary participle means 'go on doing': the participle carries the action, and the verb says only that it never stopped. ἐπίκειμαι with the dative is to lie upon a man, and so to press him hard. Tanning was foul work, and Greek cities kept tanneries at the edge of town for this reason.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ ἀεὶ αὐτὸν διανεβάλλετο λέγων μετ’ ὀλίγον χρόνον μεταβήσεσθαι.
sentences.tr: Ho de aei auton dianeballeto legōn met’ oligon chronon metabēsesthai.
sentences.l: But he always put him off, saying that after a little while he would move.
sentences.n: διαναβάλλομαι is to put a man off, defer him — the double compound strengthening the ἀναβάλλομαι that already means 'postpone'. The future infinitive μεταβήσεσθαι after λέγων keeps the tense of the words the tanner actually used.

sentences.t: Τούτου δὲ συνεχῶς γενομένου, συνέβη, χρόνου διελθόντος, τὸν πλούσιον ἠθάδα τῆς ὀσμῆς γενόμενον μηκέτι αὐτῷ διενοχλεῖν.
sentences.tr: Toutou de synechōs genomenou, synebē, chronou dielthontos, ton plousion ēthada tēs osmēs genomenon mēketi autōi dienochlein.
sentences.l: And this happening continually, it came about, time having gone by, that the rich man, having grown used to the smell, no longer troubled him.
sentences.i: This went on and on, and in time the rich man grew used to the smell and stopped troubling him.
sentences.n: ἠθάς takes the genitive of what one grows used to. Two genitive absolutes frame the main clause, the second dropped in between συνέβη and its accusative and infinitive.

sentences.t: Ὁ λόγος δηλοῖ ὅτι ἡ συνήθεια καὶ τὰ δυσχερῆ τῶν πραγμάτων καταπραύνει.
sentences.tr: Ho logos dēloi hoti hē synētheia kai ta dyscherē tōn pragmatōn katapraynei.
sentences.l: The story shows that familiarity makes gentle even the hard among things.
sentences.i: The story shows that familiarity takes the edge even off what is hard to bear.
sentences.n: Chambry prints almost this same moral at fable 42, with τὰ φοβερά, 'the frightening ones', where this has τὰ δυσχερῆ, 'the hard to deal with', and again at fable 148. καί is 'even', not 'and'; τὰ δυσχερῆ τῶν πραγμάτων is a partitive genitive under a neuter adjective. The verb is καταπραΰνω, where the υ is a syllable of its own (πραΰς, 'gentle'); the diaeresis is not printed here, and the romanization follows the word rather than the printed form.
